newsitem.title: SPAIN: Bonos shrug off rate cut and CPI, focus on EU pact.
newsitem.headline: Bonos shrug off rate cut and CPI, focus on EU pact.

text.p: Spanish government bonds, rewarded by this year's seventh official rate cut and by better than expected inflation yet again in November, shrugged off the good news at home on Friday to focus on the Dublin EU summit.
Dealers said that after all the good news in 1996 profit-taking is now a risk and increasingly so if European countries fail to reach an accord on the stability pact this weekend.
"Now that all the positive news has set in, we have the danger of profit-taking until year-end," said Robert Huw, strategist at NatWest in London.

At 1000 GMT the long term bond future was trading at around 111.16, six basis points lower from Thursday's close. Earlier today it reached 111.56 after the November CPI announcement, and then dipped to 110.92 after the central bank cut its key rate.

The Bank of Spain lowered its money market rate 50 basis points to 6.25 percent from 6.75 percent. Economists had predicted a cut either today or at the next regular repo tender on Christmas Eve. The rate started the year at nine percent.
In November, consumer prices were unchanged month-on-month for a year-on-year rise of 3.2 percent, after a rise of 0.1 percent in October for a 3.5 percent year-on-year rate.

"The CPI has developed better than expected. The Bank of Spain rate cut was to be expected with buying on the rumour when CPI came out and selling on the fact" said Antonio Mielgo, economist with Bank of America (BoA) in Madrid.

"Markets at both the short and the longer end were already pricing in the possible rate cut, and the Bank of Spain had only followed up," said Xavier Segura, chief economist at Caja de Cataluna in Barcelona.
Support came for bonos later in the shape of a comment by Italian Treasury Minister Azeglio Ciampi, who said that the EU stability pact was virtually done.
"We expect the market to remain nervous all the day, watching the Dublin summit closely," said BoA's Mielgo.
Dealers added that if the Dublin summit should fail, European bond yields would likely rise.
"If they don't reach an agreement, we'll see rates increasing everywhere in Europe, especially in the core markets," said Thierry Loiseau at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
He was expecting that the 10-year spread over Bunds could reach 100 basis points soon. It was trading at around 115 bps this morning.
But even with a possible narrowing of the spread over Bunds, bono prices were likely to drop.
"Since a couple of days ago we've seen foreign investments funds selling Spain. We are seeing people who entered last spring, or this summer, getting out," Loiseau added.
Robert Huw disagreed, however, and was expecting the peripherals to fall further than core markets if the Dublin summit should fail to come up with the goods.
"In a week's time I'd see the spread over Bunds widening toward 200 basis points for Italy and to 130 bps for Spain," Natwest's Huw said.
